newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU, Japan spirits raised by liquor tax pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU, Japan spirits raised by liquor tax pact.

text.p: The European Union and Japan have settled a long-running feud over alcohol tax after Tokyo agreed to harmonise tariffs on domestic and imported liquor within two years.
The European Commission -- the EU's executive -- said on Tuesday that Japanese tax on European spirits would be slashed in two stages while that on domestic spirits would be raised.
The news was welcomed by European spirits producers, who said they would now press for similar changes in South Korea and Chile."

"This reform provides the first opportunity for all spirits to compete on equal terms in Japan," said Gillian Darley, Director-General of the European Confederation of Spirits Producers. "It also sends out a clear signal to other countries which practise similar tax discrimination."
The EU and Tokyo have long been at odds over the tax applied to European liquor exports to the lucrative Japanese market.

Last year a World Trade Organisation disputes panel ruled against Japan in a case brought by the EU, but the Commission has been complaining that Tokyo still appeared reluctant to change the structure.

So called brown spirits -- including French cognac and Scotch whisky, are currently taxed up to 600 percent more heavily than similar domestic products while white spirits -- vodka and gin -- are taxed 250 percent higher.
Through tax cuts on imports and rises on domestic products these differences would be brought to three percent and zero respectively.
The Commission said tax on so-called Japanese Shochu A (brown) spirit would be raised to 8,076 yen ($66) per thousand litres per degree proof from 6,228 on October 1 and to 9,924 a year later.
Tax on Shochu B (white), currently at 4,084 yen would be raised to 6,028 on October 1, to 7,976 a year later and to 9,924 in 2001.
Japanese tax on imports of brown spirits -- which include whisky and brandy -- will be slashed from 24,558 yen per thousand litres per degree proof to 13,775 in October and 10,225 a year later.
Tax on imports of white spirits such as vodka and gin will be cut to 9,924 yen in October from 9,927, while tax on liqueurs will be raised to 9,924 from 8,217 at the same time.
The Commission estimated that the tax on a litre-size bottle of 40 degree proof whisky or cognac will fall from $8 to $3.5.

The volume of European alcohol sold to Japan has fallen in recent years -- a decline European producers attribute directly to the tax system. Whisky sales fell from over 14 million litres in 1994 to under 12 million in 1995.
Some 400 million European currency units ($472 million) worth of spirits were sold to Japan by the EU in 1995.

However, Japan imports relatively little of the spirits it consumes compared to other industrialised nations -- just eight percent compared to the United States (35 percent), Canada (38 percent) Germany (30 percent) and Belgium (80 percent). ($1 = 122 yen)
